g: The system on military aircraft that use either or some combination of both hydraulic and pneumatic systems.
The science of fluids made of both gas and liquid.
(Gnosticism) One of three levels of a human being, the spirit, along with the body and soul.
A pocket of air, or, figuratively, something resembling a pocket of air.
Of, relating to, or resembling air or other gases
Powered by, or filled with, compressed air
Spiritual; of or relating to the pneuma
(dated) A vehicle, such as a bicycle, whose wheels are fitted with pneumatic tyres.
(Gnosticism) In the gnostic theologian Valentinus' triadic grouping of man, the highest type; a person focused on spiritual reality (the other two being hylic and psychic).
(anatomy) Any bone, such as the mastoid process or those of the birds, that contains many hollow cells full of air
Any device which generates or is powered by compressed air.
A heavy drill consisting of a bit powered by compressed air, used e.g. for breaking tarmac.
A postal service delivering messages through pneumatic tubes.
(chemistry) A piece of laboratory apparatus, consisting of a vessel filled with liquid (generally water or mercury), used for collecting gases.
(biology) The state of being pneumatic, or of having a cavity or cavities filled with air.
the pneumaticity of the bones of birds
To convert to a pneumatic form
The branch of mechanics that deals with the mechanical properties of gases
(historical) The pneumatic postal system in Paris (abolished 1984), or a letter sent by this system.
Spiritualism centred on the belief in the pneuma.
(biology) The formation of air cavities, as in bones or a sinus
(medicine) A hernia or air-filled cyst within the lung.
(medicine) A gaseous swelling, especially within the scrotum.
The rule of the spirit in government; a spiritual approach to politics.
(marine biology) A sac or other structure containing air and used for flotation by a marine organism, chiefly used in reference to those of kelps and siphonophores.
(botany, histology) A group of cells with spiral secondary wall thickenings, present in a velamen; acts as an airway for gas exchange for respiration or photosynthesis
(botany, histology) A group of cells presumed to be specialised as an airway for ventilation of particular tissues.
(physiology) A tracing of the respiratory movements, obtained by a pneumatograph or stethograph.
An instrument for recording the movements of the thorax or chest wall during respiration.
In terms of, or by means of, pneumatology.
The study of spiritual beings and phenomena, especially the interactions between humans and God.
(Christianity, theology) The study of the Holy Spirit as revealed in Scripture.
The science dealing with air or gases, their physical and chemical properties, therapeutic applications, etc.
(geology) the alteration of rocks and minerals by gases or magmatic fluid within volcanos etc
A device used to measure the force of inspiration or expiration of a person's lungs.
A device used to measure the intraocular pressure of the eye
(zoology) A gas-filled sac or float of some colonial marine coelenterates, such as the Portuguese man-of-war.
(botany) An aerial root, in mangroves etc., specialized for gaseous exchange.
An apparatus consisting of a bag with a tube and mouthpiece, which may be attached to the body. The bag contains oxygen to be breathed by the wearer in rescue work in mines, etc.
Having or relating to a pneumatophore.
(zoology) The subumbrellar surface of siphonophorous pneumatophores.
(medicine) The abnormal accumulation of air or other gas in the body.
(medicine) The presence of undissolved gases in the urine during urination.
To activate (or become activated) within the lungs
An allergen in the lungs or respiratory tract
The presence of gas in the biliary system, typically found in patients that have recently undergone biliary surgery or endoscopic biliary procedure.
(organic chemistry) Any of a group of echinocandins produced by several fungi
(surgery) centesis of a lung, typically to remove fluid
(neurology) The presence of air inside the skull, usually caused by trauma, surgery, or other conditions that let air enter.
Of, pertaining to or caused by a pneumococcus bacterium.
(pulmonology) The infection of the lungs caused by pneumococci (Streptococcus pneumoniae).
Of, pertaining to or caused by a pneumococcus bacterium.
Any of various diseases caused by pneumococcus (for example, pneumococcal pneumonia, pneumococcal sepsis, and pneumococcal meningitis).
A gram-positive bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, that causes pneumonia and other infectious diseases.
(medicine) A colonic diagnostic procedure during which the colon is inflated with air.
radiography of the colon following introduction of air to aid contrast
(pathology) A disease of the lungs caused by inhalation of particulate matter.
(medicine) Of, relating to, or affected by pneumoconiosis.
A particular bacteriocin produced by the pneumococcus bacterium.
Synonym of pneumocystosis (which is the more common synonym)
(pathology) A parasitic fungal organism of the genus Pneumocystis, in humans specifically Pneumocystis jorevicii.
A form of pneumonia caused by the yeast-like fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A fungal infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii that primarily occurs as a pulmonary infection in AIDS patients.
A cell that is responsible for gas exchange in the alveoli in the lungs
(pathology) pneumonia in people with impaired immune systems (typically as a result of AIDS)
(zoology) Any sea angel in the family Pneumodermatidae.
An image produced by means of pneumoencephalography.
(neurology) A historical term for brain dysfunction caused by air entering the cranial cavity, typically as a complication of older diagnostic procedures like pneumoencephalography.
(biochemistry) A polysaccharide composed of pneumose and galactose residues
(anatomy) Of or pertaining to the lungs and the stomach

(anatomy) The pneumogastric nerve; one of the tenth pair of cranial nerves which are distributed to the pharynx, esophagus, larynx, lungs, heart, stomach, liver, and spleen, and, in fishes and many amphibia, to the branchial apparatus and also to the sides of the body.
(anatomy, pathology) That originates in the lungs
(medicine) A record (often overnight) of the respiratory movements of a subject by the use of pneumography.
(medicine) The presence of both air and blood in the pericardial cavity.
Any of a group of inhibitory lantibiotics produced by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
The study of the respiratory system and organs.

A putative virulence factor of the gram-positive bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae. It has a range of biological activity, including the ability to lyse and interfere with the function of cells and soluble molecules of the immune system.
(biochemistry) Any of a group of recombinant mutant proteins related to pneumolysin.
pneumatic massage of the internal portions of the ear
The condition of having the presence of air in the mediastinum.
The surgical removal of all or part of a lung.
Inflammation of the lungs caused by viruses, bacteria or other infectious microorganisms.
Of, or relating to the lungs; pulmonary.
A medicine to treat lung disease.
Any device designed for use with or relating to the lungs, such as the iron lung and medical ventilator, or any device used in the field of respiratory therapy.
A severe lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
(medicine) Of, pertaining to, or suffering from, pneumonitis.
(pathology) Inflammation of the tissue of the lungs.
The separation of an adherent lung from the pleura, to permit collapse of the lung. It was formerly used to treat tuberculosis.
(surgery) The surgical procedure of making an incision in the lung.
A disorder characterised by the presence of air in the parotid gland.
(medicine) The presence of air in the pericardial cavity.
The presence of air or gas in the peritoneal cavity.
(pathology) Peritonitis accompanied by the presence of gas in the peritoneal cavity.
(surgery) fixation of layers of the lung tissue
A bacteriophage that counters bacterial infection of the lungs
(pharmacology) That serves to protect the lungs.
(biochemistry) Any protein typically found in the fluid of the lungs
(surgery) Resection of part of a lung.
The presence of air or gas in the retroperitoneal space.
A lung spheroid that contains progenitor cells
A pore through which slugs and other gastropods breathe
A form of spirometer that measures and displays the velocity of airflow
A spirometer that measures the flow rate of gases by detecting pressure differences across the fine mesh.
Relating to the skin's ability to feel a pneumatic pulse
Pertaining to the regulation of respiratory rate.
(medicine) The treatment of disease by inhalations of compressed or rarefied gases.
(pathology) Presence of air inside the pleural cavity, usually caused by injury either to the lung or the chest wall.

An ophthalmic instrument that is used to measure the intraocular pressure using a balanced air pressure (sometimes achieved by blowing a puff of air at the cornea and measuring the subsequent flattening for the corneal surface)
A noninvasive method of estimating the intraocular pressure of the eye by exposing the cornea to a sudden puff of air
Having a toxic effect on the lungs
(anatomy) Relating to the lungs and the triceps
Having an affinity for (or moving towards) the tissues of the lungs
Any of several distinct types of microorganism present in the lungs
ventriculography of the ventricles of the larynx
Any virus of the genus Pneumovirus or of the family Pneumoviridae.
(VTuber fandom slang) A spritesheet, in PNG (Portable Network Graphics) format, containing all sprites used for a VTuber's avatar.
(transitive) To declare someone a persona non grata.
After my cover blew up I was PNGed.
A YouTube personality who uses stylized static images edited onto their videos as a substitute for a facecam.
(chemistry) Any binary compound of a pnictogen
(chemistry) Any element from group 15 of the periodic table, which includes nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony and bismuth.
(inorganic chemistry) Any binary compound containing an anion of a pnictogen; namely nitride, phosphide, arsenide, antimonide or bismuthide
(historical) A nocturnal monster in Ancient Greece that would choke its victims; incubus; nightmare.
(gene) The gene that encodes for the pinin protein
(biochemistry) pinin, the PNN protein, encoded by the PNN gene
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase, an enzyme involved in purine metabolism
Of or relating to Amir Pnueli (Hebrew: אמיר פנואלי; 1941–2009), Israeli computer scientist known for his work on temporal logic.
